extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of literary criticism, poetics, and aesthetics (readers of Aristotle/Poetics)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and explicates Aristotle's criteria for tragedy and related aesthetic principles (definition of tragedy, character requirements, katharsis, role of music, and the emotions of pity and fear) as discussed in a scholarly treatment of Poetics. Useful for evaluating or composing tragic drama in the Aristotelian tradition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aristotle's formal definition of tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Tragedy is an imitation of an action that is serious, complete, and of a certain magnitude; in language embellished with each kind of artistic ornament, the several kinds being found in separate parts of the play; in the form of action, not of narrative; through pity and fear effecting the proper katharsis, or purgation, of these emotions.’ (Poetics vi.2)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This single formulation bundles the genus (imitation), the qualities of the action (serious, complete, magnitude), the modes of presentation (embellished language; different ornaments used in different parts), the formal mode (dramatic action, not narrative), and the purposive effect (katharsis of pity and fear). Each clause implies an evaluative requirement for tragic composition and criticism. The text further unpacks 'several kinds of embellishment' (verse in dialogue; lyrical song in choral parts) and stresses that catastrophe must be presented as action, not mere narration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seriousness / nobility (ozovéaias) of the action
rubrics_metrics.description: The action imitated in tragedy must be 'serious' or 'noble'—i.e., neither ludicrous nor morally trivial; it must concern a significant human destiny or well-being (eudaimonia).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The word ozovéaias carries both gravitas and greatness; translations like 'noble' risk over-emphasising moral quality alone. Tragedy is concerned with a grave, significant picture of human destiny; the action should not be ludicrous or petty. This distinguishes tragedy from comedy (the latter imitates lower, often ludicrous characters).

rubrics_metrics.name: Completeness and certain magnitude of the action
rubrics_metrics.description: The tragic action must be complete (a whole with a beginning, middle, end) and of a certain magnitude (sufficient scope/importance and, for some commentators, appropriate duration).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Completeness implies structural unity and causal coherence so the plot is a whole. 'Magnitude' refers to the significance and scale of the action (some interpreters also read a temporal/length dimension). Critics (e.g., Addison) have read 'magnitude' as including duration, but Aristotle's intent is primarily about significance and scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form: dramatic action not narrative
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy must be presented in the form of action (dramatic enactment), not as narrated description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This distinguishes tragedy from epic poetry: tragedy unfolds through enacted scenes and dialogue (drama), whereas epic relies on narrative recounting. Evaluation should favor showing rather than telling when assessing tragic composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language and the several kinds of embellishment
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy employs embellished language with several kinds of artistic ornament, distributed in different parts of the play (verse in dialogue; lyrical song in choral parts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle himself explains these embellishments: verse without music for dialogue, lyrical song for the chorus. These choices are part of the formal criteria: assess whether the play uses appropriate linguistic/metrical and musical resources in the parts suited to them. This also differentiates tragedy from other mixed forms (e.g., nomic or dithyrambic poetry).

rubrics_metrics.name: Catharsis (katharsis) through pity and fear
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy's specific function is to effect the proper katharsis (purgation/clarification) of the emotions of pity and fear, by arousing them and bringing about a resulting emotional effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The term katharsis admits medical, religious, and moral metaphors; interpretations vary (medical purgation, homoeopathic relief, moral purification). The Poetics deficiency on this point forces recourse to Politics. Evaluation should consider both the arousal and the subsequent alleviation/transformation of pity and fear, not mere moral edification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Katharsis: multiple senses and mechanism (medical, religious, aesthetic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Katharsis can be read as (1) medical purgation (removal of morbid element), (2) religious/liturgical purification or expiation, and (3) moral purification; as applied to tragedy it likely combines psychological relief with an aesthetic principle of purification/clarification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scholarly readings (e.g., Bernays) emphasize a homoeopathic, medical metaphor: tragic excitation of pity and fear affords pleasurable relief and temporary quieting of morbid emotion. The book argues katharsis both as psychological relief and as an artistic clarification that purifies and transmutes disturbing elements of pity/fear into higher, refined feeling. When evaluating a tragedy, consider whether it effects such a transformation, not simply whether it morally edifies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Music's specific role in katharsis and distinct uses of music
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain types of music (tumultuous melodies) serve a kathartic function—curing religious or emotional 'enthusiasm' by applying movement to cure movement—distinct from music used for moral education, relaxation, or aesthetic enjoyment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle (via Politics) distinguishes four uses of music; the kathartic music is a physical stimulus providing an outlet for religious fervour and leads patients back to a normal state. In tragedy, choral music may perform this kathartic work. Evaluation should note whether musical elements contribute specifically to the purgation/clarification of emotion rather than merely ornamenting the piece.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character goodness: heroic/noble order (not mere plain virtue)
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters in epic and tragic poetry possess 'goodness' of a heroic or elevated order—distinct from plain, unaspiring virtue—so that their imperfections still impress imagination and evoke grandeur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle allows moral imperfections that enhance imaginative grandeur; the required 'goodness' is not ordinary virtue but a form of moral grandeur that elevates the action. However, greatness (mere power or fame) cannot substitute for goodness—e.g., sheer greatness in villainy (Satan) fails Aristotelian tests for a fitting tragic protagonist. Evaluation should weigh whether a character's qualities arouse the sense of grandeur and moral seriousness required by tragedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral nobility required, not mere outward rank
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle requires moral nobility (worthiness, capacity for significant action) in tragic actors rather than merely high social rank; the French tradition's emphasis on princes/kings as necessary tragic protagonists is a misreading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text stresses that outward social rank is neither necessary nor sufficient; what matters is the capacity of a life to yield a great and significant action. When assessing suitability of characters for tragedy, discriminate between genuine moral/tragic nobility and mere aristocratic status or courtly decorum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction of aesthetics from moral didacticism: end is refined pleasure/delight
rubrics_metrics.description: The end (telos) of poetry is a refined pleasure or delight; moral teaching (the utile) may accompany poetry but cannot replace its primary aesthetic function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle severs aesthetics from the earlier didactic view that poetry's main office is ethical instruction. While moral effects may result, a poet fails if the work does not produce the proper pleasure. Critical assessment should prioritize aesthetic efficacy (eliciting appropriate delight and emotional effect) even when moral instruction is present.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pity and fear: Aristotelian psychological definitions and interrelation
rubrics_metrics.description: Fear is a species of pain or disturbance arising from the impression of impending destructive or painful evil that is near and threatens us; pity is a pain at an evident destructive evil happening to someone undeserving, where we could imagine it happening to ourselves—pity and fear are correlated, and inability to feel fear implies inability to feel pity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle's analysis grounds the tragic emotions in self-regarding instincts: pity contains an implicit reference to self (we imagine ourselves in the other's plight). Evaluating tragic impact should consider whether the work elicits these precisely related emotions (pity & fear) as Aristotle defines them, not a generic compassion unlinked to self-regard.
